analysis.one_liner: Eases workers' proof of job discrimination and extends civil rights law to congressional employees.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 16, 1990 with six Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the same day and never received a hearing or vote before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it easier for workers to prove job discrimination by letting them use statistical evidence that a hiring or promotion practice has a lopsided racial, sex, or religious effect, unless the employer proves a business necessity. It would also have let discrimination be one major contributing factor rather than the sole reason for a job decision, added a monetary award of up to $100,000 where back pay cannot make a victim whole, covered expert witness fees, and restored protection against discrimination in carrying out contracts. It would also have applied federal employment discrimination law to congressional employees, who were then exempt from it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination based on race, sex, religion, or national origin: they could win cases with statistical proof of a disparate impact, without having to show discrimination was the only reason for a decision, and could recover expert fees and up to $100,000 in extra money where back pay cannot be awarded. People denied fair treatment in carrying out existing contracts, victims of hidden discriminatory seniority systems, and congressional employees would also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Lets a worker prove discrimination by showing with statistical evidence that an employment practice has a disparate impact by race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, shifting the burden to the employer to justify the practice as a business necessity [S2][S3].

Makes discrimination unlawful when race, sex, religion, or national origin is a major contributing factor to an employment decision, even if other factors also contributed, rather than requiring it to be the sole reason [S2][S3].

Authorizes a court to order an employer to pay up to $100,000 in cases of intentional discrimination where back pay cannot be awarded and more is needed to deter future violations, and includes expert witness fees in attorney's fee awards so victims can afford to build a case [S2][S3].

Restores protection against private discrimination not just in making a contract but in its performance, breach, modification, or termination, closing a gap left by the Supreme Court's 1989 Patterson v. McLean Credit Union decision [S2][S3].

Allows challenges to seniority systems adopted for a discriminatory purpose even when that purpose is hidden inside the system, and applies Title VII employment discrimination law to congressional employees for the first time [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face a lower burden of proof in disparate-impact cases, attorney's and expert fees, and awards of up to $100,000 in intentional-discrimination cases where back pay is unavailable. Congress itself, as an employer, would lose its exemption from the employment discrimination law it applies to everyone else.

drawbacks.text: It caps the additional monetary award at $100,000 and requires all Title VII issues to be decided by a judge rather than a jury, far weaker remedies than the rival Civil Rights Act of 1990 that allowed unlimited compensatory and punitive damages [S3].

It exempts rules barring employment of people who knowingly use or possess illegal drugs from disparate-impact challenges unless the rule was adopted with intent to discriminate, shielding blanket drug screens from statistical scrutiny [S2][S3].

It bars many later challenges to employment practices required by litigated or consent judgments, meaning workers who had notice of such a decree but were not parties to it could not attack practices it locked in [S2][S3].

Its business-necessity standard accepts practices whose goals are merely 'significantly served' by the challenged practice, a looser employer defense than the strict-necessity standard civil rights groups sought [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill offered real but deliberately modest gains: clearer statistical proof standards, fee coverage, and a capped monetary remedy, while trading away the stronger tools in the rival bill, such as unlimited damages and jury trials, to win broader acceptance. The cost fell on employers through easier lawsuits and fee exposure, and on Congress as an employer. The larger problem is that even this compromise version never advanced, so workers got none of its protections; Congress instead pursued the stronger S. 2104, which passed both chambers but was vetoed, and no employment-discrimination fix became law that Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Nancy Kassebaum introduced the bill on July 16, 1990, with Senators Gorton, Wilson, and Murkowski as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day [S5].
The action record shows nothing after the referral: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

The Senate was instead advancing a stronger, rival Civil Rights Act of 1990 (S. 2104) that same month, which passed both chambers; President George H.W. Bush vetoed it in October 1990 and the Senate sustained the veto, so no employment-discrimination remedy bill became law that year (widely reported).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead: the Republican compromise that would have eased discrimination lawsuits died in committee, and the stronger rival bill passed by Congress was vetoed, leaving workers with none of the new remedies either version offered.

for.name: Nancy Kassebaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 16, 1990 as a Republican-authored alternative to strengthen federal employment discrimination law

for.name: Slade Gorton, Pete Wilson, and Frank Murkowski
for.role: U.S. Senators (R-WA, R-CA, R-AK), original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined Kassebaum in introducing the bill in the Senate

against.name: Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never took up the bill after referral; the action record shows no hearing, markup, or vote, as the committee worked on the rival, stronger S. 2104 instead

against.name: George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the stronger rival Civil Rights Act of 1990 (S. 2104) in October 1990, ending that year's civil rights effort; he never acted on this alternative, which never reached his desk

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its sponsor and all six cosponsors were Senate Republicans (6 of 45), while the rival stronger bill that did reach the floor drew mostly Democratic support and a Republican presidential veto (widely reported).

industries.note: The bill would have made it substantially easier for employees to win discrimination cases, with statistical proof of disparate impact, attorney's and expert fees, and awards of up to $100,000 where back pay cannot remedy the harm. Employers' interest in limiting such liability runs directly against the workers the bill protects.

Title VII would have applied to Congress itself for the first time, ending the exemption of congressional offices from the employment discrimination law they impose on private employers. Congressional employees would have gained a remedy their peers in the executive branch and private sector already had.
